title: Mini-Project: Synthetic A/B Test With scipy.stats
prompt: Run Welch's t-test (equal_var=False) on group_a = [10, 12, 11, 13, 12] and group_b = [16, 18, 17, 19, 18]. Store the p-value as p_val (float) and set significant = bool(p_val < 0.05).
solution:
from scipy import stats
group_a = [10, 12, 11, 13, 12]
group_b = [16, 18, 17, 19, 18]
_, p_raw = stats.ttest_ind(group_b, group_a, equal_var=False)
p_val = float(p_raw)
significant = bool(p_val < 0.05)
explanation: Welch's t-test compares two independent sample means without assuming equal variances.
starterCode:
from scipy import stats
group_a = [10, 12, 11, 13, 12]
group_b = [16, 18, 17, 19, 18]
# Compute p_val and significant
visibleTests:
assert isinstance(p_val, float)
assert significant is True
assert p_val < 0.001

title: What p-value means
prompt: Recall the definition of a p-value.
solution: Probability of observing data at least as extreme as the sample, assuming the null hypothesis is true.
back: The probability of observing results at least as extreme as your sample **assuming the null hypothesis (H0) is true**.

title: Why report effect size
prompt: Recall why p-values alone are insufficient.
hints: Large N makes tiny differences significant
solution: Large samples can produce tiny p-values for practically meaningless differences.
front: Why should you always report effect size alongside a p-value?
back: With large sample sizes, even trivial differences can yield `p < 0.05`; effect size shows whether the difference matters in practice.
